messages.body_plain:
That's quite strange, I can't seem to reproduce your error with the following code. Could you modify the following to better reflect your dataset and reproduce the error?

library(mirt)

set.seed(12345)
a <- matrix(abs(rnorm(15,1,.3)), ncol=1)
d <- matrix(rnorm(15,0,.7),ncol=1)
itemtype <- rep('2PL', nrow(a))
N <- 1000
dataset1 <- simdata(a, d, N, itemtype)
dataset2 <- simdata(a, d, N, itemtype, mu = .1, sigma = matrix(1.5))
dat <- rbind(dataset1, dataset2)
group <- sample(1:3, size = N*2, replace=TRUE)
models <- 'F1 = 1-15'

mod_configural <- multipleGroup(dat, models, group = as.character(group))
coef(mod_configural, simplify=TRUE)

Phil

That's odd you'd get a convergence error in M2. The only model that gets estimated there is the null model where all the slopes are all set equal to 0, which only affects statistics like CFI and TLI. I'm not quite sure how well the 2PLNRM null model converges, but it's possible the intercept only forms are too unstable to estimate (it's rare, but not outside the range of possibilities). You might just want to rely on the M2 statistics and RMSEA, and just pass calcNull = FALSE to avoid this error. HTH.

Phil

The change happened in this commit: https://github.com/philchalmers/mirt/commit/aec5ab95a850040e06a172de94c6307974f00be7

The initial form used some incorrect summations, resulting in a collapsed table of derivatives that were incorrect. Overall, this resulted in some conservative estimates for C2, making models appear better than they should have, which I did not notice right away (this was detected by a few others who use mirt, and was therefore patched immediately). The results now give the anticipated behavior in terms of Type I error control and power.

As a general rule, brand new features should be treated as alpha releases since they could potentially have bugs that I was not aware of yet. The longer something has been in the package though, the better tested it is, and therefore the more trustworthy. That principle is true of most software, so open-source is no different. Cheers.

Phil

messages.subject: Re: formative factor
messages.subject_clean: formative factor
messages.body_plain:
IRT models are best understood as reflective, in that the latent trait is the reason why the observations behave the way they do (i.e., why some individuals respond differently than others because of their latent trait location). Formative models are really (linear) composites intended to represent stand-ins of definition constructs; hence, the causal arrows are in the other direction (SES is a good example of this, where we define things that jointly combine to reflect what we mean by SES....not that SES somehow exists outside the variables). I don't know of a good application in IRT where this makes sense, because we nearly always understand item responses as being manifestations of something underlying the test in the form of a construct.

That all said, if you do have an application of this there's really no need to use IRT to create this formative construct. As exogenous variables in the SEM framework have no distributional assumptions, and therefore can represent categorical variables, you can just obtain your formative by using packages such as lavaan. And because the constructs are defined without error (linear aggregates in this case) it's easy to just create these constructs as new variables and utilize these in other analyses, such as in the IRT framework. HTH.

Phil

messages.body_plain:
Dear Phil,

I've been reading a paper (DOI: 10.3102/1076998618825116) where authors propose an iterative procedure to detect aberrant responses in a sample of test takers. Just to summarize the important points, this is what the procedure looks like:

1. Estimate item parameters on the full sample
2. Flag participants whose person-fit statistic is below the cutoff
3. Estimate item parameters on the reduced sample (without flagged participants). Use those item parameters from the REDUCED sample to compute person parameters from the FULL sample
4. Repeat 2 & 3 until the difference in the percentage of flagged participant in the current and previous iteration is less than 0.01

Now, my question: the authors in the linked paper use a lz* statistic of person fit. I am wondering do you think it would be possible to use the Zh statistic from your package to follow the same procedure? Are you aware of any theoretical and/or mathematical reasons that would prevent this usage? As far as I know, the lz* statistic is used only for binary items and I am interested in detecting aberrant responses on Likert scales.

messages.subject_clean: Detecting aberrant responses using person fit statistics
messages.body_plain:
I also am not aware of the polytomous generalization to this statistic, though it could very well be that nobody has generalized it yet. The PerFit package contains a number of these person-fit type indices, so you might have some luck there.

Regarding the paper, the approach these authors took is a pretty aggressive one, and reminds me a lot of fitting regression models after iteratively removing all cases that have even minimally large residuals. An alternative strategy, which doesn't require the standardized lz* versions of the statistic, is to apply a weight function to each response vector according to these person fit measures.

E.g., compute the original model, obtain Zh for each case (or lz*), and obtain the weight w = 1/abs(Zh). Given this weight vector, pass the result to the survey.weight input to re-estimate the model to obtain a model that is less influenced by the originally contaminated observations. Under this approach, cases that are initially deemed unusual get progressively less weight in the final model. You could obviously repeat this process if you wanted to, but in the end it has the same effect (and in the limiting case where the w -> 0 in really unusual cases then this is equivalent to removing the observations entirely. Hence, the data removal approach is a limiting subset of this weighted approach). HTH.

Phil

Hi all,

I am new to IRT, so I apologise if this is a very basic question!

I am seeking to provide information on item "difficulty" for a GPCM mirt model (featuring 3 items, 2 of which are binary and 1 which has levels 1-8). I am working with a large-scale secondary dataset collected in Tanzania. (Discrimination between categories is not great for the multi-level item, but all levels have been retained as I need to do everything possible to distinguish between individuals!)

I am able to give the most likely theta level for each individual within my dataset given their score for each item:
model2015 = mirt(data = IRTset2015, model = 1, itemtype = "gpcm", na.rm = F)
Original2015set$fsmaths <- fscores(model2015, method = "EAP", na.rm = F) #provides theta levels for each individual within the original dataset

But, is it possible to obtain a difficulty level for each individual item (and each category within my multi-level item)? Conceptually, I think that would entail calculating the theta level at which an individual had a 50% chance of success for a binary item. For my multi-level item, however, I am not so sure. I think the points that I need numbers for are the top of the peaks for levels 2-7 and the P=0.5 point for levels 1 and 8. (I might just be wrong here though!) I have provided trace plots from my model below:

Please let me know if there is any way of getting this information. The following commands do not appear to provide it:

summary(model2015) #provides F1 and h2
coef(model2015) #provides a1 (discrimination), akX (item levels) and d1 (which does not appear to be the information that I am after either)

Thanks in advance for any help. This would be greatly appreciated,

Joe

Run the coef function in mirt to print your item parameters estimated from the model. You will have one b parameter for binary items. This is the item difficulty for that item. Keri

Thanks Keri,

Having done a bit more looking on the collapsing of categories, research suggests that as "there were no simulation conditions for which collapsing of categories significantly improved the estimation of the latent trait, the collapsing of categories is not advisable under any preventable circumstance" (http://digitool.library.mcgill.ca/webclient/StreamGate?folder_id=0&dvs=1553098171390~937, p. 79). messages.body_plain:
I think your interpretation is wrong here. For the partial credit modeling family the 'difficulty' parameters are really the theta locations where adjacent probability lines intersect; hence, they are not constrained to be strictly ordered (as would be the case for the graded response model, for example). Here's a stock example using some data from the package:

library(mirt)
dat <- expand.table(Bock1997)
dat2 <- dat
dat2[,1] <- ifelse(dat[,1] == 1, 2, dat2[,1])
dat2[,1] <- ifelse(dat[,1] == 2, 1, dat2[,1])
mod <- mirt(dat2, 1, 'gpcm')
coef(mod, IRTpars=TRUE)
itemplot(mod, 1)

Which gives the output from coef():

$`items`
           a     b1     b2    b3
Item.1 0.456  0.026 -0.194 0.957
Item.2 0.957 -1.702 -0.192 0.948
Item.3 0.777 -1.526 -0.058 0.020

Notice that the difficulty parameters are not ordered. Each one of these values does describe where the adjacent categories functions intersect though. P1-P2 intersect at 0.026, P2-P3 at -0.194, P3-P4 at 0.957. The GPCMs are ordered according to their internal scoring coefficients, so they are being scored as though they are ordered, but this doesn't necessarily imply the intersections of the probability functions will be ordered.

Phil

It's possible to define the item response stimuli using artibrary HTML code, or the HTML tags avilable in shiny and other packages. For example,

 # help(tags, package='shiny')
 options <- matrix(c("Strongly Disagree", "Disagree", "Neutral", "Agree", "Strongly Agree"),
                   nrow = 3, ncol = 5, byrow = TRUE)
 shinyStems <- list(HTML('Building CATs with mirtCAT is difficult.'),
                div(HTML('mirtCAT requires a'), br(), HTML('substantial amount of coding.')),
                div(strong('I would use'), HTML('mirtCAT in my research.')))
 questions <- sapply(shinyStems, as.character)
 df <- data.frame(Question=questions,
                  Option = options,
                  Type = "radio",
                  stringsAsFactors=FALSE)

 res <- mirtCAT(df)
 res

Unless you are referring to other package in the interface, but these also will accept similar definitions (e.g., lastpage() is a function called to generate the last page in its entirety).

Re: final_fun() is called just before the last page has been rendered (it's used for saving and such, so on the off chance the last page crashes at least the results would save correctly).

Phil
